---
title: "Validating the methods of Leibold et al. (2010) and Peres-Neto et al. (2012)"
---

The functions `phylo_vector()`, `trait_partition()` and `node_test()` are translations of MATLAB code from the
supplements of these articles. We checked them in three ways. Each help page lists the
differences between the text of the article and the code.

## Comparison with the original code

We ran the MATLAB code in Octave on the numerical example of Appendix A of Peres-Neto et
al. (2012) and on simulated data. The supplement lacks the functions `eigen` and
`WeightedMeanVar`, which we wrote. Weighted coordinates, correlations, Moran's eigenvector
maps and the raw and adjusted fractions agreed to within 1e-13. Correlations also agreed
with `ade4::fourthcorner()`. The package does not include the maps, as those of
`adespatial::dbmem()` are the same as the ones of the supplement.

## Type I error and power

The script `data-raw/validation_gradient.R` follows the simulations of the article, with
1000 data sets and 999 permutations (100 sites and 50 species, one environmental variable).
The article stacks the two null distributions and uses alpha / 2, shown here as "stacked".
Rates near 0.05 are expected for a true null hypothesis, with a standard error near 0.007.

Trait and environment (Table 4 of the article), with the correlation inside
`phylo_vector()`. The package has no function for this test, which is available in
`ade4::fourthcorner()`:

| Case | Tolerance | Row, article | Row, here | Column, article | Column, here | Stacked, article | Stacked, here | Larger p, here |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Random trait | 1 | 0.836 | 0.812 | 0.056 | 0.050 | 0.030 | 0.048 | 0.050 |
| Random trait | 20 | 0.916 | 0.923 | 0.052 | 0.042 | 0.046 | 0.042 | 0.042 |
| Random trait | 60 | 0.984 | 0.985 | 0.058 | 0.048 | 0.048 | 0.047 | 0.048 |
| Random environment | 1 | 0.052 | 0.053 | 0.678 | 0.695 | 0.052 | 0.052 | 0.053 |
| Random environment | 20 | 0.056 | 0.052 | 0.832 | 0.866 | 0.038 | 0.051 | 0.052 |
| Random environment | 60 | 0.058 | 0.046 | 0.954 | 0.962 | 0.036 | 0.046 | 0.046 |

Global test of `phylo_vector()`, with one Brownian trait:

| Case | Tolerance | Stacked, article | Stacked, here | Larger p, here |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Random environment (Table 1) | 1 | 0.028 | 0.039 | 0.051 |
| Random phylogeny (Table 2) | 1 | 0.042 | 0.040 | 0.040 |
| Power (Table 3) | 1 | 0.880 | 0.875 | 0.877 |
| Power (Table 3) | 20 | 0.948 | 0.934 | 0.936 |
| Power (Table 3) | 60 | 0.948 | 0.940 | 0.941 |

With tolerances of 20 and 60, which the article does not report for Tables 1 and 2, the
larger p-value gave rates from 0.037 to 0.055. The test of the final vector after a
significant global test kept these rates, because the global test comes first. A test of
that vector alone is not valid, as it was chosen to fit the predictor.

### Weights of the eigenvectors

The correlation between the vector and the trait that generated the data depends on how
the eigenvectors are weighted. The text uses correlations and the code their absolute
values.

| Tolerance | PEV with absolute values, here | PEV in Table 3 | PEV with signs, here | PEV-B, here | PEV-B in Table 3 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0.480 | 0.514 | 0.685 | 0.698 | 0.676 |
| 20 | 0.455 | 0.526 | 0.722 | 0.707 | 0.703 |
| 60 | 0.473 | 0.508 | 0.740 | 0.715 | 0.688 |

Absolute values give about what the article reports for PEV, which suggests that its Table
3 used them (this is our interpretation). With signs, PEV matches PEV-B, so the gain of the
Brownian vectors reported in the article may come from this difference.

### Partition

Table 5 uses the logistic generator of Appendix C. The appendix leaves out the intercepts and
the scale of the slopes, so we took them from the simulation code of Ives & Helmus (2011):
intercepts from N(0, 0.5), slopes with a standard deviation of 1 among species, and presences
from a uniform draw. Neither the article nor the appendix says how the two vectors were
obtained. The fractions of Table 5 agree with the vectors that generated the data, and its
rejection rates for E and S agree with the global test of `phylo_vector()`, so the table
below combines both (`data-raw/validation_table5.R`, 1000 data sets, 999 permutations). The
values of the article are in parentheses:

| Scenario | [E, S] | [a] | [b] | [c] | Rejection of E | Rejection of S |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| I | 0.490 (0.478) | 0.223 (0.216) | 0.043 (0.069) | 0.223 (0.193) | 0.706 (0.687) | 0.710 (0.679) |
| II | 0.473 (0.589) | 0.008 (0.061) | 0.458 (0.488) | 0.007 (0.036) | 0.700 (0.750) | 0.705 (0.751) |
| III | 0.383 (0.349) | 0.239 (0.234) | 0.030 (0.036) | 0.114 (0.079) | 0.691 (0.701) | 0.592 (0.418) |
| IV | 0.047 (0.032) | 0.023 (0.015) | 0.000 (0.001) | 0.024 (0.016) | 0.043 (0.051) | 0.047 (0.061) |
| V | 0.524 (0.457) | 0.219 (0.202) | 0.049 (0.054) | 0.255 (0.201) | 0.683 (0.597) | 0.724 (0.637) |
| VI | 0.518 (0.440) | 0.217 (0.201) | 0.051 (0.063) | 0.251 (0.176) | 0.707 (0.632) | 0.697 (0.627) |
| VII | 0.549 (0.396) | 0.255 (0.194) | 0.041 (0.000) | 0.253 (0.202) | 0.700 (0.562) | 0.708 (0.597) |

The pattern among scenarios is the same, and scenarios I, III and IV are the closest. Three
choices are ours. In scenario III, the N(0, 1) error of Appendix C has no effect on a gradient
from -15 to 15, so we added it to `y` with unit variance, and only in the analysis. In
scenarios V and VI, `x` is in random order along the transect, as otherwise it is correlated
with space. In scenario II we kept the text, and the gradients seem more correlated than those
of the article, as fractions `a` and `c` are smaller.

Three parts remain different. The share of the compositional component is near 0.62 in all
scenarios, whereas the article gives 0.39 to 0.94, so that value must depend on something
that the appendix does not describe. Scenario VII has a larger `b` than the zero of the
article, probably because the maps here are orthogonal only without site weights. The
rejection of [E, S] is 0.71 to 0.91, against 0.77 to 0.84, here as the rejection of either
gradient, which gives 0.085 in scenario IV against 0.055 in the article. Rejections of `a` and
`c`, with vectors estimated only after a significant global test, were 0.66 to 0.71 and 0.48
to 0.72 outside scenarios II and IV, against 0.56 to 0.70 and 0.30 to 0.60 in the article; in
scenario II they were zero, against 0.29 and 0.25.

Following the demonstration script of the authors instead, with a vector fixed in advance and predictors
without relation to the data, rejection rates of the larger p-value were 0.023 to 0.028,
because both null hypotheses are true. With environment and space acting, the global test
for environment passed in 37% of the data sets. In those, the rejection rate was 0.99 for
fraction `a` and 0.03 for fraction `c`, as expected for a vector estimated for environment
alone.

### Tests of the fractions

The code of the authors permutes environment and space with the same order of sites and
compares fractions `a` and `c` themselves with their null values, so each is compared with
what is expected when neither set matters. The fraction is not a pivotal statistic: when the
other set explains much, the observed fraction is a share of what that set leaves, and the null
fraction is a share of everything, so the test loses its power. Up to version 0.6.0 the package
did the same; `trait_partition()` now tests `a` and `c` with the share of the component that the other set
leaves unexplained, which is a monotone function of the partial F statistic, under the same
permutations (Anderson & Legendre 1999 found that permutation of raw data with a pivotal
statistic has the right size except with outliers in the covariable). The shared fraction `b`
is tested with `shared_null`, following `adespatial::envspace.test()` (Bauman et al. 2019):
`env` is replaced by surrogates that keep its spatial autocorrelation, built by Moran spectral
randomisation (Wagner & Dray 2015) or by moves of the whole map on a grid, while the response
and `space` stay fixed.

The script `data-raw/validation_fractions.R` measures type I error and power on a complete
grid of 8 by 8 sites, with `space` holding the six broadest Moran's eigenvector maps, 20 species
with Gaussian responses to a gradient that combines the environment (weight alpha) and a smooth
field in the span of `space` (weight beta), 199 permutations and 500 data sets per scenario,
with seeds separate from the 200 data sets used to choose the statistic and the null models.
The environment is independent noise (iid), a smooth field in the span of `space` plus noise
(broad), or a field at scales that `space` does not hold (fine). In the last scenario the
composition follows another trait than the one analysed, so the null hypothesis of the
permutation of species is true for every fraction. Rates at the 5% level have standard errors
of 0.010 or less; a true null hypothesis is marked by an asterisk.

Fractions `a` and `c`, with the fraction (old) and the share left by the other set (new) as
statistic, by free permutations of sites, by moves of the whole map with
`torus_permutations()` (grid), by permutations of species, and with the larger p-value of sites
and species:

| Scenario | [a] old, sites | [a] new, sites | [a] new, grid | [a] new, species | [a] new, larger p | [c] old, sites | [c] new, sites | [c] new, grid | [c] new, species | [c] new, larger p |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Neither acts, env iid | 0.062* | 0.052* | 0.052* | 0.074* | 0.040* | 0.044* | 0.042* | 0.060* | 0.068* | 0.038* |
| Space acts, env iid | 0.000* | 0.058* | 0.078* | 0.072* | 0.044* | 1.000 | 1.000 | 1.000 | 1.000 | 1.000 |
| Space acts, env broad | 0.000* | 0.056* | 0.082* | 0.058* | 0.042* | 1.000 | 1.000 | 0.986 | 1.000 | 1.000 |
| Env acts, env iid | 1.000 | 1.000 | 1.000 | 1.000 | 1.000 | 0.000* | 0.038* | 0.190* | 0.040* | 0.022* |
| Env acts, env broad | 1.000 | 1.000 | 1.000 | 1.000 | 1.000 | 0.000* | 0.100* | 0.000* | 0.028* | 0.024* |
| Both act, env broad | 0.818 | 1.000 | 1.000 | 1.000 | 1.000 | 0.962 | 1.000 | 0.948 | 1.000 | 1.000 |
| Weak env and space, env broad | 0.150 | 1.000 | 0.998 | 0.998 | 0.998 | 0.996 | 1.000 | 0.980 | 1.000 | 1.000 |
| Space acts, env fine | 0.000* | 0.114* | 0.014* | 0.056* | 0.040* | 1.000 | 1.000 | 1.000 | 1.000 | 1.000 |
| Env acts through another trait | 0.360* | 0.454* | 0.442* | 0.062* | 0.062* | 0.096* | 0.172* | 0.034* | 0.074* | 0.064* |

The old test never rejected `a` when space acted and the environment did not, nor `c` in the
mirror case, and had little power for a weak effect of the environment beside space. The new
statistic holds the level there and in the tuning run gave the same rates as permutation of
the residuals of the reduced model (Freedman & Lane 1983) and as permutation of the predictor
of interest alone, which do not support `site_permutations` and the permutation of species.
Three limits remain. When the environment has spatial structure at scales that `space` does not
hold, the free permutation of sites rejects `a` too often (0.114), because the residuals keep
spatial structure that the environment matches by chance; moves of the whole map hold the
level (0.014). When a strong, spatially structured environment acts alone, the free permutation
rejects `c` in 10% of the data sets: the species respond to the environment with Gaussian
curves, the linear fit leaves a spatially structured remainder, and space explains it, which
the larger p-value does not take as significant (0.024). The moves of the map are nearly
degenerate for `c`, because moving Moran's eigenvector maps rigidly on the grid changes little
of what they explain, and the test of `c` with `site_permutations` was liberal when the
environment explained much (0.190) and never rejected when the environment was spatially
structured. With a trait unrelated to the composition, the permutation of sites rejects `a` in
about half the data sets and the larger p-value holds the level, as intended. The permutation
of species alone, with 20 species, is slightly liberal when nothing acts (0.066 to 0.080 with
either statistic), and the larger p-value is not.

A second generator (`data-raw/validation_fractions_check.R`: counts, a grid of 10 by 10 sites,
8 Moran's eigenvector maps, 200 data sets) gave larger values for these two limits. With a
hidden field that `space` holds only in part, free permutations rejected `a` in 21% of the data
sets (larger p-value: 2%), and with a structured environment acting alone they rejected `c` in
25% (larger p-value: 7.5%). So `p_max`, not the p-value of sites alone, is the one to read.

The shared fraction `b`, with `env` replaced by free permutations of its values, by Moran
spectral randomisations (MSR, `shared_null = "msr"`) and by moves of the whole map
(`shared_null = "sites"` with `torus_permutations()`), by permutations of species, and with
the larger p-value. `Tested` is the number of data sets, out of 500, where `env` was related to
`space` and `b` was tested with the MSR:

| Scenario | Tested | [b] free env | [b] MSR | [b] grid | [b] species | [b] larger p, MSR | [b] larger p, grid |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Neither acts, env iid | 22 | 0.043* | 0.045* | 0.045* | 0.000* | 0.000* | 0.000* |
| Space acts, env iid | 28 | 0.103* | 0.000* | 0.097* | 0.643* | 0.000* | 0.097* |
| Space acts, env broad | 500 | 0.476* | 0.056* | 0.110* | 0.770* | 0.056* | 0.110* |
| Env acts, env iid | 15 | 1.000 | 1.000 | 1.000 | 1.000 | 1.000 | 1.000 |
| Env acts, env broad | 500 | 1.000 | 1.000 | 1.000 | 1.000 | 1.000 | 1.000 |
| Both act, env broad | 500 | 0.898 | 0.432 | 0.618 | 0.926 | 0.432 | 0.618 |
| Weak env and space, env broad | 500 | 0.634 | 0.282 | 0.272 | 0.748 | 0.282 | 0.272 |
| Space acts, env fine | 0 | | | | | | |
| Env acts through another trait | 500 | 0.786* | 0.542* | 0.678* | 0.048* | 0.048* | 0.050* |

`b` is left untested when `env` is unrelated to `space` at the 5% level, which happened in
94% to 97% of the data sets with an iid environment and in all those with structure outside
`space`; the rates above leave those data sets out, and with fewer than 30 of them they say
little. With an environment that is spatially structured but has no effect, free permutations
of `env` reject `b` in 48% of the data sets, the Moran spectral randomisation holds the level
(0.056), and moves on the grid are liberal (0.110), which we did not expect and leave as a
limit of that null model. The permutation of species asks whether the trait matters, not whether the shared
structure is spurious, so it rejects when space acts through the trait; conversely, with a trait
unrelated to the composition, the randomisation of `env` alone rejects often and only the
larger p-value holds the level. Power is complete when the environment alone acts and moderate
when space also acts on its own.

## The daphniids of Leibold et al. (2010)

The data set `daphniids` rebuilds the data of the article from the public survey. With the
larger p-value, no predictor is significant at any node, as species permutations have
little power with 13 species. The article permutes rows and columns together, which
`node_test()` gives as `p_joint`. Rates of rejection per node at the 5% level (one Yule
tree of 24 species, 60 sites, 300 data sets, 99 permutations, `data-raw/validation_node.R`):

| What acts | Sites | Species | Larger p | Joint |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Neither | 0.053 | 0.049 | 0.021 | 0.050 |
| Environment | 0.777 | 0.049 | 0.049 | 0.764 |
| Phylogeny | 0.046 | 0.050 | 0.021 | 0.050 |
| Both | 0.803 | 0.073 | 0.073 | 0.795 |

The joint test is valid only when neither acts. With the environment alone it behaves as
the permutation of sites, so it does not separate an effect of the environment from an
association between environment and phylogeny.

In the daphniids, the joint test with 999 permutations found fewer predictors than sites
alone at the 0.05 level (PHEQ, AV_DEP, DOC, TN_TP and PTL at four nodes, with none left
after the false discovery rate). It therefore did not recover Figure 3a better. With sites
alone, at a level of 0.05 without correction and 999 permutations, environmental results
compare with Figure 3a as follows:

| Node | Figure 3a | Here |
|---|---|---|
| *retrocurva*, *parvula*, *catawba* | COND, NTL | COND, NTL |
| Same plus *pulicaria*, *pulex* | AV_DEP, PHEQ | AV_DEP, PHEQ |
| *longispina*, *galeata*, *rosea* | AV_DEP, ELEV | AV_DEP, ELEV |
| All species | TN:TP, AV_DEP, ELEV, DOC, COLOR | COLOR, DOC, AV_DEP |
| All *Daphnia* except *laevis*, *dubia* | AV_DEP, PHEQ, ELEV, DOC | AV_DEP, PHEQ, ELEV, DOC, NTL, TN_TP |
| Clade with *ambigua* | ELEV | ELEV, TN_TP |
| *retrocurva*, *parvula* | PHEQ, AV_DEP | AV_DEP |
| *pulicaria*, *pulex* | ELEV, NTL | none |
| *galeata*, *rosea* | COLOR, DOC | none |
| *laevis*, *dubia* | COND | NTL, PHEQ, PTL, TN_TP |

Nodes with rare species differ most: *D. laevis* and *D. rosea* occur in one and two lakes
of the rebuilt set. Biogeographic results differ more (no match at most nodes), which we
expected, because the article does not give the area of each lake and we approximated
rivers by longitude.
